authoredSolutions.21: For a one-electron species \(E_{n}=-13.6\frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}\ \mathrm{eV}\). For \(\mathrm{He^{+}}\), \(Z=2\): \(E_{2}=-13.6\times\frac{4}{4}=-13.6\ \mathrm{eV}\) and \(E_{3}=-13.6\times\frac{4}{9}=-6.04\ \mathrm{eV}\). The difference is \(E_{3}-E_{2}=13.6\times4\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right)=13.6\times\frac{5}{9}=7.56\ \mathrm{eV}\), which matches option (C), 7.54 eV.
authoredSolutions.23: The key, (a), ranks the three complexes by the field strength of the ligand, \(\mathrm{CN^-} > \mathrm{H_2O} > \mathrm{Cl^-}\), which is the order of the ENERGY of the light each absorbs (the size of \(\Delta\)). It is not the order of how strongly each absorbs, which is what "intensity of colour" means. Square planar \([\mathrm{Ni(CN)_4}]^{2-}\) (\(dsp^2\), diamagnetic) is only pale yellow in solution, while tetrahedral \([\mathrm{NiCl_4}]^{2-}\), which has no centre of symmetry, absorbs more strongly than a complex that has one. The stem also prints no charges. The key follows the setter's reading (intensity taken as \(\Delta\)); do not use this question to learn what controls intensity.
authoredSolutions.24: Gallium (\(Z=31\)) is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{2}4p^{1}\). Forming \(\mathrm{Ga^{+}}\) removes the outermost \(4p\) electron, leaving \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{2}\). The valence electrons of \(\mathrm{Ga^{+}}\) are therefore the \(4s\) electrons, for which \(l=0\), option (A). The trap is \(l=1\): that is the \(4p\) electron of neutral Ga, and it is the one removed.
authoredSolutions.25: Ruhemann's purple, the violet product of the ninhydrin test, exists as a resonance-stabilised anion; the structures shown in (a) and (c) are equivalent resonance contributors of the same species. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.26: An ester reacts with two equivalents of a Grignard reagent — the first gives a ketone, the second adds to it. Ethyl ethanoate \(CH_3COOC_2H_5\) with \(2\,CH_3MgBr\) gives \((CH_3)_3COH\) (2-methylpropan-2-ol). So 2 equivalents are needed. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.28: This is a metallurgy question (refining of metals), not the purification of an organic compound. Metals with low boiling points are refined by distillation: zinc (b.p. about 1180 K) is vaporised away from less volatile impurities and condensed. Iron, copper and nickel boil far higher (above 2800 K) and are refined in other ways (electrolysis for copper, Mond's process for nickel). So zinc is the metal purified by distillation, option (C).
authoredSolutions.29: Xenon has 8 valence electrons. In \(XeOF_{4}\) two of them go into the \(Xe=O\) double bond, one into each of the four \(Xe-F\) bonds, and the remaining two form one lone pair. Xenon therefore has 5 \(\sigma\) bonds (four to F, one to O) and 1 lone pair: steric number 6, \(sp^{3}d^{2}\) hybridisation, square pyramidal shape. The \(\pi\) bond to oxygen does not count towards the hybridisation. Option (C).
authoredSolutions.30: In \(I_3^-\) the central iodine has 5 electron domains (\(sp^3d\)): 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs, giving a linear ion. So there are 3 lone pairs on the central atom. Hence option (D).
authoredSolutions.31: Classify each hydroxide. \(Be(OH)_{2}\) and \(Al(OH)_{3}\) are both amphoteric: they dissolve in acids and in alkalis. \(B(OH)_{3}\) (boric acid) is a weak monobasic acid; it acts as a Lewis acid, accepting \(OH^{-}\) from water. \(H_{3}PO_{3}\) is also an acid. \(NaOH\) and \(Ca(OH)_{2}\) are both bases. Only in pair (B) do the two differ: \(B(OH)_{3}\) is acidic while \(Al(OH)_{3}\) is amphoteric. Option (B).
authoredSolutions.32: For the equimolar liquid, \(x_{\text{benzene}} = x_{\text{toluene}} = 0.5\). Raoult's law gives the partial pressures \(p_{\text{benzene}} = 0.5\times70 = 35\) and \(p_{\text{toluene}} = 0.5\times20 = 10\), so the total is 45. By Dalton's law the mole fraction of benzene in the vapour is \(y = \frac{35}{45} = 0.78\), option (b), 0.77. The vapour is richer than the liquid in the more volatile benzene.
authoredSolutions.35: A carbocation is resonance-stabilised when the positive charge sits next to a \(\pi\) bond or lone pair (allylic/benzylic), allowing the charge to delocalise. The cation in option (B) has such an adjacent \(\pi\) system. Hence option (B).
authoredSolutions.38: Disproportionation needs an intermediate oxidation state, so the element can be both oxidised and reduced. Bromine is \(+1\) in \(\mathrm{BrO^-}\), \(+3\) in \(\mathrm{BrO_2^-}\) and \(+5\) in \(\mathrm{BrO_3^-}\), all intermediate. In \(\mathrm{BrO_4^-}\) bromine is \(+7\), its highest state, so it can only be reduced and cannot disproportionate. Option (D).
authoredSolutions.39: \(\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}\) is a strong dehydrating agent and removes water from nitric acid: \(\mathrm{4HNO_3 + P_4O_{10} \rightarrow 2N_2O_5 + 4HPO_3}\), exactly the 1 : 4 ratio. The nitrogen oxide formed, \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\), is the anhydride of nitric acid and is acidic. Option (A).
authoredSolutions.40: Cold dilute \(KMnO_{4}\) (Baeyer's reagent) adds two OH groups syn across the double bond of cyclohexene, giving A = cyclohexane-1,2-diol. Hot acidic \(KMnO_{4}\) cleaves the double bond and oxidises both carbons to COOH, opening the ring to B = hexane-1,6-dioic acid (adipic acid). Option (A) is the intended answer, although it names A 'cyclohexane-1,6-diol': carbons 1 and 6 of a six-membered ring are neighbours, so the correct name is cyclohexane-1,2-diol.
